issues.issue: The parenthetical defining the employee party is broken off mid-phrase ("You," "you," "your," or "Fy and your heirs and successors), so it is unclear whether heirs and successors are themselves parties or merely covered. The same sentence binds "affiliates and successors" of the Company without identifying which affiliates.

"[T]he Company determines ... that the services are substantially complete" uses an undefined standard — neither "services" nor "substantially complete" is defined anywhere in the Agreement, and the determination is left to the Company alone. A court could be asked what services were owed and when they became substantially complete.

The promise to pay $60,300 is made "subject to the terms and conditions of this Agreement," but §7 gives the Company sole and absolute discretion over interpretation and §12 lets it terminate the Agreement at any time, so the payment obligation's content only emerges from reading those provisions together. A court could be asked whether §1 confers any enforceable right at all once §7 and §12 are given effect.

The provision turns on "IBAS terms" and "the provisions of IBAS (including appropriate reductions for hypothetical tax)," an acronym and document never defined or attached to the Agreement. What tax result an IBAS assignee gets is therefore unascertainable from the instrument.

This clause says the Payment "may be affected by a change in your duties or position as set forth below," while §2(a) mandates that a transfer out of the initial position "will be" prorated. The permissive "may be affected" cannot be squared with §2(a)'s automatic proration.

"Company initiated severance" is undefined, and the clause does not say whether an involuntary discharge for cause, a reduction in force, or a constructive discharge falls within it. That term alone decides whether a prorated Payment is owed.

Read with §4, which lets the Company terminate employment "with or without cause and with or without notice," and §2(b), which forfeits on resignation or retirement, the Agreement leaves an involuntary termination that is not a "severance" unprovided for. A court would have to decide which of the two regimes such a termination falls under.

"[R]esignation or retirement (other than retirement in connection with a Company initiated severance)" leaves the boundary between a voluntary resignation and a Company-driven departure undrawn, and does not carve out a resignation connected to a severance the way it carves out retirement. Whether a departure is a resignation or a severance under §2(a) decides forfeiture.

Forfeiture turns on the Company's conclusion that "you failed to meet performance expectations in your assignments and responsibilities," a standard with no defined benchmark and no stated process, and ground (vi) forfeits for violating the Code of Conduct "in any respect." A court could be asked whether any objective limit constrains the Company's conclusion.

The proviso applies "in the case of certain leaves of absences" without identifying which leaves, and says the unpaid amount "may" be accelerated, leaving the trigger and the obligation both indeterminate. The parenthetical list of leaves ("military or sick leave, ... to enter governmental employment") is also incomplete on its face.

The bar on transfer runs "until the Agreement has expired," but the Term provision allows the Agreement to be "satisfied" on an early date and §12 allows termination, so it is unclear when expiration occurs for this purpose. The exception for will and descent also sits oddly with §2(a)'s direct payment to the estate.

The Company's reserved right to terminate employment at any time "with or without cause" stands against §2(a), which promises a prorated Payment on a Company-initiated severance, and §2(b)/(c), which forfeit it. A court would have to say whether a no-cause termination triggers §2(a) proration or merely the at-will reservation here.
